articles.heading: Application of the FIDE Laws of Chess Online
articles.content:
The FIDE Laws of Chess apply to online chess competitions except where modified by the FIDE Online Chess Regulations (E04). Online chess competitions must be conducted on FIDE-approved or recognised platforms.

The regulations are structured in three parts:
- Part I (Arts 1–5): Basic Rules of Play — applicable to all online competitions
- Part II (Arts 6–7): Regulations for Online Competitions — general
- Part III a (Arts 8–15): Regulations for Online Competitions with Supervision
- Part III b (Arts 16–20): Regulations for Hybrid Chess Competitions

The arbiter retains all authority as in over-the-board play. Technical issues specific to online play are governed by the specific articles within E04.

All official FIDE online competitions must also comply with the FIDE Fair Play Rules for Online Competitions with Supervision (Appendix I of E04).

articles.heading: Playing Zone
articles.content:
The playing zone is the physical location where a player competes in a supervised online event. Requirements:

- The playing zone must have a stable internet connection adequate for the platform used
- Adequate lighting for video monitoring of the player's face and playing area
- No unauthorised persons may be present in the playing zone during the game
- The player's computer screen must not be visible to unauthorised persons
- The playing zone must be quiet and free from distractions

A player may not leave the playing zone during their game without the arbiter's permission, mirroring the over-the-board rule (Article 11.2 of the Laws of Chess).

For competitions where players are in a central supervised venue (hub), the hub constitutes the playing zone and is subject to all the standards that apply to an over-the-board playing area.

For remote supervised competitions (players play from home or other locations), the player must ensure their playing zone meets the minimum requirements specified by the arbiter and announced in the tournament regulations.

articles.heading: Moving the Pieces on the Virtual Chessboard
articles.content:
A move is considered made when it is executed on the virtual board and confirmed by the platform. Key differences from over-the-board play:

Touch-move rule: The touch-move rule (Article 4 of the Laws) does NOT apply to online play. A player may select and deselect a piece without penalty until the move is confirmed by clicking or releasing the piece on the target square.

Completed move: A move is completed when:
- It is registered on the platform's server, and
- The player's clock has been pressed (or automatically switched)

Cancellation: Once a move is confirmed (executed and clock pressed), it cannot be taken back. If a technical error causes an incorrect move to be registered, the arbiter must investigate immediately and may restore the position.

Pre-moves: The use of pre-moves (moves queued in advance) is permitted in online play unless the tournament regulations specifically prohibit them.

Promotion: When a pawn reaches the last rank, the promotion piece must be selected before the move is confirmed. If the platform automatically promotes to a queen and the player intended a different piece, the arbiter must be notified immediately.

articles.heading: Virtual Chessclock
articles.content:
The virtual clock is controlled automatically by the platform. The clock starts when the game begins and switches after each confirmed move.

Clock discrepancies: If there is a discrepancy between the displayed time and the actual elapsed time due to a platform error, the arbiter has authority to investigate and may adjust the time. Players must report clock issues to the arbiter immediately — delayed reports may not be accepted.

Lag and connection delay: Some platforms apply a lag compensation. The specific lag compensation used must be announced in the tournament regulations. Excessive lag that significantly affects the game may be grounds for the arbiter to pause the game.

Time controls: All FIDE-approved time controls (increment, delay, simple time limits) may be used in online competitions. The platform must support the required time control.

Flag fall: In online play, the platform determines flag fall automatically. A player whose time expires loses the game unless:
- The position is such that the opponent cannot checkmate by any series of legal moves (in which case it is a draw), or
- The game has already been decided (checkmate, resignation, or draw agreement)

articles.heading: General Provisions for Online Competitions with Supervision
articles.content:
For online competitions with supervision (Part III a), the following general provisions apply:

- The event must be supervised by an appointed arbiter throughout
- The arbiter must be familiar with the platform and its monitoring capabilities
- A monitoring software (Fair Play software) must be used — the only FIDE-authorised tool is the FIDE Game Screening Tool, unless another tool is explicitly approved by FIDE FPL
- Players must agree to the conditions of the online competition (camera requirements, screen sharing, etc.) as a condition of entry
- Prizes should not be awarded until Fair Play checks have been completed

For competitions where players play from separate locations (remote), the arbiter monitors all games through the platform's monitoring tools and video feeds. The arbiter may also have assistants monitoring specific games or boards.

The competition regulations must specify:
- The platform to be used
- Camera and microphone requirements
- Permitted and prohibited items in the playing zone
- Procedures for disconnections and technical issues
- The appeals procedure

articles.heading: Players' Conduct in Online Competitions with Supervision
articles.content:
In supervised online competitions, players must comply with the following conduct requirements:

Camera requirements:
- The player must keep their camera on at all times during the game
- The face must be clearly visible and well-lit
- The camera must not be moved or covered during the game without the arbiter's permission

Playing environment:
- No chess-related material (books, notes, databases) may be visible in the player's environment
- The player must not have any other device (tablet, phone, second computer) active in the playing zone
- Mobile phones must be switched off or placed out of reach and view of the camera

Screen sharing:
- Players may be required to share their screen so the arbiter can verify no prohibited software is running
- The player must be able to display their computer's task manager or equivalent on request

Behaviour:
- Players may not consult any person, book, or electronic device during the game
- Players may not leave their seat without informing the arbiter
- Players may not communicate with others during the game except as permitted by the regulations

Violations may result in the loss of the game, disqualification from the event, or further disciplinary action.

articles.heading: The Arbiter's Role in Online Competitions
articles.content:
The arbiter in an online competition has all the powers of an over-the-board arbiter, adapted for the online environment:

Monitoring: The arbiter monitors all games through the platform's monitoring tools and video feeds. The arbiter should be able to see all games at all times.

Pausing games: The arbiter has authority to pause, resume, or terminate a game due to:
- Technical issues (platform malfunction, disconnection)
- Fair play violations
- A player's medical emergency
- Any other reason requiring intervention

Fair play: The arbiter is responsible for implementing fair play measures. If a player is found to have violated the conduct rules, the arbiter may declare the game lost for that player. All fair play incidents must be reported to the Chief Arbiter and, where required, to the Fair Play Commission.

Decisions: The arbiter's decisions are final within the event, subject to the appeals procedure. A decision must be made promptly to minimise disruption to the game.

Screening: The arbiter sends all games in PGN format to the FIDE Game Screening Tool (or equivalent approved tool) and acts on any findings. Screening should occur during and after the event.

articles.heading: Disconnections
articles.content:
If a player is disconnected from the platform during a game:

1. The player's clock continues to run during the disconnection.
2. The player must reconnect as quickly as possible.
3. If the disconnection lasts longer than the time specified in the tournament regulations, the arbiter may declare the game lost for the disconnected player.
4. Repeated disconnections by the same player may be treated as misconduct, especially if they occur at critical moments of the game (e.g. when the player is in a losing position).

First disconnection: A brief disconnection (within the threshold) is treated as a technical issue and the game continues after reconnection.

Long disconnection: If the disconnection exceeds the threshold, the arbiter decides the outcome based on:
- The nature of the disconnection (technical failure vs. voluntary disconnection)
- Whether the player can prove the disconnection was involuntary (e.g. internet outage evidence)
- The position on the board at the time of disconnection

The threshold time and procedures must be specified in the tournament regulations before the event begins. A common threshold is 3–5 minutes.

If both players disconnect simultaneously, the arbiter investigates and determines the appropriate action.

articles.heading: Hybrid Chess Competitions — General Provisions
articles.content:
A hybrid chess competition is one in which some players are physically present in a central playing venue while other players participate remotely from different locations.

Key characteristics:
- The same FIDE Laws of Chess apply to all players regardless of location
- Over-the-board (OTB) players and remote players compete under the same rules, adapted for the hybrid format
- Special arrangements must be made for remote players to observe the game in real time
- Remote players must be able to communicate with the arbiter easily

Special arrangements required:
- Electronic boards must be used for OTB players so that moves are transmitted in real time to remote players
- The remote player's interface must clearly show the position and time remaining for both players
- Video conferencing must be available so the arbiter can communicate with remote players

Arbiter's role in hybrid events:
- The Chief Arbiter must appoint at least one dedicated arbiter for remote players
- The remote arbiter monitors the video feeds and platform of remote players
- The OTB arbiter handles any issues at the physical playing venue
- Both arbiters must be in communication throughout the event

Hybrid events have more complex technical requirements than either fully OTB or fully online events. The organiser should conduct a technical rehearsal before the event to verify all systems are functioning.

articles.heading: Glossary of Terms in the FIDE Online Chess Regulations
articles.content:
Key terms specific to online chess:

Hub: A physical location where players in an online competition play from a central supervised venue.

Hybrid competition: A competition combining over-the-board play at a central venue with remote online participants.

Lag: Delay in data transmission between the player's device and the platform server. May affect the displayed time on the clock.

Platform: The online software system used to conduct the games (e.g. Lichess, chess.com, Chess24, FIDE Online Arena).

Playing device: The computer, tablet, or other device used by the player to play.

Pre-move: A move made by a player before their opponent's move is confirmed, which is automatically executed when it becomes the player's turn.

Remote play: A player competing from a location other than the central playing venue.

Screen sharing: A feature of video conferencing software that allows the arbiter to view the player's computer screen in real time.

Task manager: Software on a player's computer that shows all running processes, used by the arbiter to verify no prohibited software is active.

Video conferencing system: The software used for real-time video monitoring of players (e.g. Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet).
